For $n\in\mathbb Z$, define $|n|=n$ if $0\le n$ and $|n|=-n$ if $n<0$, using the integer order and additive inverse of [[def-int-order]] and [[def-int-operations]]. Totality and compatibility of the integer order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]) give $0\le|n|$ and $-|n|\le n\le|n|$. Adding these bounds for $m,n\in\mathbb Z$ gives $|m+n|\le|m|+|n|$. Equip $\Gamma$ with the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty(x,y)=\max_{1\le r\le d}|x_r-y_r|$; the maximum exists because the coordinate set is finite and nonempty, symmetry and separation hold coordinatewise, and the absolute-value triangle inequality gives $|x_r-z_r|\le|x_r-y_r|+|y_r-z_r|$ for every coordinate, hence the triangle inequality for $d_\infty$. A **finite region** is a finite subset $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$; its cardinality is $|\Lambda|$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]).

For a finite region $\Lambda$, let $S_\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,q\}^{\Lambda}$ be the set of spin configurations on $\Lambda$. Induction on $|\Lambda|$ gives $|S_\Lambda|=q^{|\Lambda|}$: the empty region has one configuration, and for $x\in\Lambda$ the restriction map $s\mapsto(s|_{\Lambda\setminus\{x\}},s(x))$ is a bijection $S_\Lambda\to S_{\Lambda\setminus\{x\}}\times\{1,\ldots,q\}$, so adjoining one site multiplies the number of configurations by $q$, according to the recursion defining natural-number powers in [[def-nat-power]]. Let $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ be the vector space of functions $f:S_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}f(s)\overline{g(s)}$. For each $s\in S_\Lambda$, let $e_s$ be the indicator function of $\{s\}$; these vectors form an orthonormal basis. For $\Lambda=\varnothing$, $S_\Lambda$ is a singleton and $\mathcal H_\Lambda\cong\mathbb C$. The **local spin matrix algebra** is

$$\mathcal A_\Lambda:=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)\cong M_{q^{|\Lambda|}}(\mathbb C),$$

Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms of the finite-dimensional Hilbert space; they are bounded. The algebra has composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity $I_\Lambda$, and induced operator norm

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

The **finite local trace** is $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(T):=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}\langle T e_s,e_s\rangle$ in the displayed configuration basis $(e_s)$. This is the usual finite-matrix trace; basis independence and its cyclic/unitary identities are supplied by [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]].

If $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, restriction of configurations gives the canonical factorization $\mathcal H_{\Lambda'}\cong\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes\mathcal H_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$, with sites ordered lexicographically. The **factor inclusion** is the unital $*$-homomorphism $\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}:\mathcal A_\Lambda\to\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}$ given by $T\mapsto T\otimes I_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$. A **localization region** for $T$ is any finite $\Lambda$ for which $T\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ under these inclusions; a localization region need not be minimal.

The ordinary operator norm makes each local matrix algebra a nonzero unital complete C*-algebra, and every positive normalized complex-linear functional is uniquely a trace pairing with a density matrix, by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]]. This includes the empty region, whose Hilbert space is $\mathbb C$. This definition does not posit an infinite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert space.

Fix $d\ge1$, the site set $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, its max-coordinate metric $d_\infty$, and the local spin algebras $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ of the uniformly finite-dimensional spin system. A finite interaction is a family $\Phi(Z)=\Phi(Z)^*\in\mathcal A_Z$ indexed by finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$. For a finite $\Lambda\subset\Gamma$, define

$$H_\Lambda^\Phi:=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi(Z),\qquad \tau_t^{\Lambda,\Phi}(A):=e^{itH_\Lambda^\Phi/\hbar}Ae^{-itH_\Lambda^\Phi/\hbar},$$

where $\hbar>0$, $A$ is embedded in a common finite local algebra, and the finite sum is a self-adjoint matrix. When a path $\Phi_s$, $s\in[0,1]$, is used, each $\Phi_s(Z)$ is $C^1$ in matrix norm and the derivative is taken term by term.

For $r\ge0$ put $F(r)=(1+r)^{-d-1}$. The admissible weights used here are

$$F_a(r):=e^{-ar}F(r)\quad(a>0),\qquad F_\rho(r):=(1+r)^{-\rho}\quad(\rho>d).$$

For an admissible weight $G$, define the weighted interaction norm

$$\|\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma}\frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{\substack{Z\subset\Gamma\ {\rm finite,\ nonempty}\\x,y\in Z}}\|\Phi(Z)\|.$$

The derivative norm of a path is

$$\|\partial\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma} \frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{Z\ni x,y}|Z|\,\|\partial_s\Phi_s(Z)\|.$$

A finite-volume spectral band is a nonempty selected subset $\Sigma_\Lambda(s)\subseteq\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})$ together with the orthogonal projection onto the sum of its eigenspaces. It may be specified by an interval $I_\Lambda(s)$ with smoothly varying endpoints, in which case $\Sigma_\Lambda(s)=\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})\cap I_\Lambda(s)$. The band is uniformly isolated with gap $\gamma>0$ along a specified finite-volume exhaustion when

$$\operatorname{dist}\!\left(\Sigma_\Lambda(s),\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})\setminus\Sigma_\Lambda(s)\right)\ge\gamma$$

for every volume in that exhaustion and every $s\in[0,1]$. For spectral-flow arguments, the selected eigenvalues must also form a locally fixed spectral cluster: for each $s_0$, a contour in the resolvent set encloses exactly the selected eigenvalues for all $s$ in a neighborhood of $s_0$. In finite dimension this implies that its projection is $C^1$ when the Hamiltonian path is $C^1$. This cluster condition holds, for example, for the first $r_\Lambda$ eigenvalues counted with multiplicity when the integer $r_\Lambda$ is fixed along the path and the gap after them stays open. Uniform distance between the selected and unselected spectra alone does not prevent an interval from changing membership discontinuously. A ground band is such a band containing the lowest eigenvalue or a finite-volume cluster of lowest eigenvalues; no uniqueness is implicit.

For physical units, take interaction terms and Hamiltonians in joules, time in seconds, and $\hbar$ in joule-seconds. The path parameter $s$, lattice distance, and admissible weights are dimensionless; the interaction norm therefore has energy units and the derivative norm has energy units per dimensionless path parameter.

where $\hbar>0$, $A$ is embedded in a common finite local algebra, and the finite sum is a self-adjoint matrix. When a path $\Phi_s$, $s\in[0,1]$, is used, each $\Phi_s(Z)$ is $C^1$ in matrix norm and the derivative is taken term by term.

$$F_a(r):=e^{-ar}F(r)\quad(a>0),\qquad F_\rho(r):=(1+r)^{-\rho}\quad(\rho>d).$$

$$\|\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma}\frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{\substack{Z\subset\Gamma\ {\rm finite,\ nonempty}\\x,y\in Z}}\|\Phi(Z)\|.$$

The derivative norm of a path is

$$\|\partial\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma} \frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{Z\ni x,y}|Z|\,\|\partial_s\Phi_s(Z)\|.$$

Let $a>0$ be the weight parameter and $v=2C_{F_a}\sup_s\|\Phi_s\|_{F_a}$, with $V=1+v$. For $z\in\Lambda_n\setminus Y_k$, the supports $Y$ and $\{z\}$ are disjoint; [F3] and the local-expectation estimate [F4] give $\left\|\tau_t^{\Lambda_n,\Phi_s}(\Phi'_s(Y)) -E_{Y_k}^{(n)}\tau_t^{\Lambda_n,\Phi_s}(\Phi'_s(Y))\right\| \le C|Y|\|\Phi'_s(Y)\|e^{v|t|}e^{-ak/2},$ where the lattice shell count and the exponential factor in $F_a$ give one constant $C$ independent of $Y,n,s,t$. The same difference is at most $2\|\Phi'_s(Y)\|$ by contractivity. Split the filtered integral at $T_k=ak/(4V)$. On $|t|\le T_k$ the first bound is at most $C|Y|\|\Phi'_s(Y)\|e^{-ak/4}$; on $|t|>T_k$, the Schwartz-tail construction in [F2] gives $\int_{|t|>T_k}|W_\gamma(t)|dt\le C_N(1+k)^{-N}$ for each $N$. Since $\Delta^k_{Y,n}$ is a difference of the (k)- and $(k-1)$-expectations, its norm is bounded by the sum of these two expectation errors. Thus, after increasing $C_N$, for every $N$ there is a constant $C_N$ independent of $Y,n,s,k$ such that $\|\Delta^k_{Y,n}(s)\|\le C_N|Y|\|\Phi'_s(Y)\|(1+k)^{-N}.$ For $k=0$, the same estimate with an enlarged $C_N$ follows from $\|E_Y(B_{Y,n})\|\le\|W_\gamma\|_1\|\Phi'_s(Y)\|$.

The finite-range path has a uniform range $R$, so $x,y\in Y_k$ implies $d_\infty(x,y)\le R+2k$. Also [F1] at $x=y$ gives $\sup_s\sum_{Y\ni x}|Y|\|\Phi'_s(Y)\|<\infty$. Since $x\in Y_k$ forces $Y\cap B_k(x)\ne\varnothing$, the sum of $|Y|\|\Phi'_s(Y)\|$ over such $Y$ is at most $C(k+1)^d$. For each fixed $s$, summing the shell estimate from step 2.1 over all $Y,k$ with $x,y\in Y_k$ gives $\sum_{\substack{Z\subseteq\Lambda_n\\x,y\in Z}}\|\Psi_{\Lambda_n}(Z,s)\| \le C_N\sum_{k\ge (d_\infty(x,y)-R)/2}(1+k)^{d-N}.$ For any prescribed $\rho>d$, choose $N>\rho+d+1$; the last tail is bounded by $C_\rho(1+d_\infty(x,y))^{-\rho}$. The bound is independent of $s$ and $n$, so taking their suprema outside the support sum proves the stated uniform $F_\rho$-norm bound. No sum of separate time suprema is asserted; all finite-volume sums are finite and their nonnegative shell bounds are dominated by the displayed convergent scalar series.

Fix a finite support $Z$. Once $\Lambda_n$ contains the $(2\operatorname{diam}Z+1)$-neighborhood of $Z$, any shell with support $Y_k\cap\Lambda_n=Z$ has $Y\subseteq Z$ and $k\le\operatorname{diam}Z$; otherwise $Y_k\cap\Lambda_n$ would contain a point in that neighborhood outside $Z$. Thus only finitely many pairs $(Y,k)$ contribute to $\Psi_{\Lambda_n}(Z,s)$, and their shell projections are the fixed $E_{Y_k}$ once $n$ is large. By [A1], [F6], and [F5], for each fixed $s$, $\tau_t^{\Lambda_n,\Phi_s}(A)$ converges locally uniformly on compact $t$-intervals. The same boundary estimate in the proof of [F5] is uniform in $s$, because the path has uniform finite range and interaction bounds. For $A=\Phi'_s(Y)$, uniformity over $s$ follows by covering the compact finite-dimensional set $\{\Phi'_s(Y):s\in[0,1]\}$ by a finite norm net and using contractivity of the dynamics. The tails $|t|>T$ are bounded uniformly by $2\sup_s\|\Phi'_s(Y)\|\int_{|t|>T}|W_\gamma(t)|dt$, which tends to zero by [F2]. Hence every contributing filtered term converges uniformly in $s$, defining $\Psi_\infty(Z,s)$. The $F_\rho$-norm bound passes to the limit by taking the limit on each finite set of support terms and then the supremum.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix $d\ge1$, the site set $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, its max-coordinate metric $d_\infty$, and the local spin algebras $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ of the uniformly finite-dimensional spin system. A finite interaction is a family $\Phi(Z)=\Phi(Z)^*\in\mathcal A_Z$ indexed by finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$. For a finite $\Lambda\subset\Gamma$, define

$$H_\Lambda^\Phi:=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi(Z),\qquad \tau_t^{\Lambda,\Phi}(A):=e^{itH_\Lambda^\Phi/\hbar}Ae^{-itH_\Lambda^\Phi/\hbar},$$

where $\hbar>0$, $A$ is embedded in a common finite local algebra, and the finite sum is a self-adjoint matrix. When a path $\Phi_s$, $s\in[0,1]$, is used, each $\Phi_s(Z)$ is $C^1$ in matrix norm and the derivative is taken term by term.

For $r\ge0$ put $F(r)=(1+r)^{-d-1}$. The admissible weights used here are

$$F_a(r):=e^{-ar}F(r)\quad(a>0),\qquad F_\rho(r):=(1+r)^{-\rho}\quad(\rho>d).$$

For an admissible weight $G$, define the weighted interaction norm

$$\|\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma}\frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{\substack{Z\subset\Gamma\ {\rm finite,\ nonempty}\\x,y\in Z}}\|\Phi(Z)\|.$$

The derivative norm of a path is

$$\|\partial\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma} \frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{Z\ni x,y}|Z|\,\|\partial_s\Phi_s(Z)\|.$$

A finite-volume spectral band is a nonempty selected subset $\Sigma_\Lambda(s)\subseteq\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})$ together with the orthogonal projection onto the sum of its eigenspaces. It may be specified by an interval $I_\Lambda(s)$ with smoothly varying endpoints, in which case $\Sigma_\Lambda(s)=\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})\cap I_\Lambda(s)$. The band is uniformly isolated with gap $\gamma>0$ along a specified finite-volume exhaustion when

$$\operatorname{dist}\!\left(\Sigma_\Lambda(s),\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})\setminus\Sigma_\Lambda(s)\right)\ge\gamma$$

for every volume in that exhaustion and every $s\in[0,1]$. For spectral-flow arguments, the selected eigenvalues must also form a locally fixed spectral cluster: for each $s_0$, a contour in the resolvent set encloses exactly the selected eigenvalues for all $s$ in a neighborhood of $s_0$. In finite dimension this implies that its projection is $C^1$ when the Hamiltonian path is $C^1$. This cluster condition holds, for example, for the first $r_\Lambda$ eigenvalues counted with multiplicity when the integer $r_\Lambda$ is fixed along the path and the gap after them stays open. Uniform distance between the selected and unselected spectra alone does not prevent an interval from changing membership discontinuously. A ground band is such a band containing the lowest eigenvalue or a finite-volume cluster of lowest eigenvalues; no uniqueness is implicit.

For physical units, take interaction terms and Hamiltonians in joules, time in seconds, and $\hbar$ in joule-seconds. The path parameter $s$, lattice distance, and admissible weights are dimensionless; the interaction norm therefore has energy units and the derivative norm has energy units per dimensionless path parameter.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $H_\Lambda(s)$ be the finite-volume self-adjoint matrix of a $C^1$ interaction path on the dimensionless parameter $s\in[0,1]$, and let the selected spectral band be a locally fixed spectral cluster, separated from its complement by $\gamma>0$ uniformly in $s$, in the sense of the interaction definition. Choose a positive reference energy $E_0$ and measure physical energies in units of $E_0$; $H_\Lambda$, $H'_\Lambda$, and $\gamma$ in this statement are dimensionless, and the Fourier evolution uses $\hbar=1$. Let $P_\Lambda(s)$ be the orthogonal spectral projection onto that band. Then $P_\Lambda$ is $C^1$. There is a real, odd, integrable function $W_\gamma\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, with Fourier convention

$$\widehat W_\gamma(\omega):=\int_{\mathbb R}W_\gamma(t)e^{it\omega}\,dt,$$

such that $\widehat W_\gamma(\omega)=i/\omega$ whenever $|\omega|\ge\gamma$, and for every integer $N\ge0$ there is $c_N<\infty$ with

$$\int_{|t|>T}|W_\gamma(t)|\,dt\le c_N(1+T)^{-N}\qquad(T\ge0).$$

The finite matrix

$$D_\Lambda(s):=\int_{\mathbb R}W_\gamma(t)e^{itH_\Lambda(s)} H_\Lambda'(s)e^{-itH_\Lambda(s)}\,dt$$

is self-adjoint and satisfies

$$P_\Lambda'(s)=i[D_\Lambda(s),P_\Lambda(s)].$$

Assume Countable Choice and the finite-matrix $C^*$-identity for the local spin algebras. Let $\Phi_s$, $s\in[0,1]$, be a $C^1$ finite-range interaction path on $\mathbb Z^d$, with uniform range, support-cardinality, weighted interaction norm, and weighted derivative norm as in the interaction definition. Assume the selected finite-volume bands along a fixed increasing exhaustion $\Lambda_n\uparrow\mathbb Z^d$ are locally fixed spectral clusters with uniform gap $\gamma>0$. Let

$$D_{\Lambda_n}(s)=\int_{\mathbb R}W_\gamma(t)\, \tau_t^{\Lambda_n,\Phi_s}\!\left(H'_{\Lambda_n}(s)\right)\,dt,$$

where energies are dimensionless ($\hbar=1$) and $W_\gamma$ and the filtered derivative are as in the finite-volume spectral-generator lemma. For every $\rho>d$, there are self-adjoint local interactions $\Psi_{\Lambda_n}(Z,s)$, supported in $Z\subseteq\Lambda_n$, such that

$$D_{\Lambda_n}(s)=\sum_{Z\subseteq\Lambda_n}\Psi_{\Lambda_n}(Z,s),\qquad \sup_n\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\|\Psi_{\Lambda_n}(s)\|_{F_\rho}<\infty.$$

For every fixed finite $Z\subset\mathbb Z^d$, the coefficient $\Psi_{\Lambda_n}(Z,s)$, set to zero when $Z\not\subseteq\Lambda_n$, converges in norm uniformly in $s$ to a self-adjoint $\Psi_\infty(Z,s)$. The limiting interaction has finite $F_\rho$-norm for every $\rho>d$.

For every finite $\Lambda_n$ and support $Z\subseteq\Lambda_n$, the coefficient $s\mapsto\Psi_{\Lambda_n}(Z,s)$ is norm-continuous.

Let $G$ be either $F_a$, $a>0$, or $F_\rho$, $\rho>d$, as in the weighted-interaction definition. Let $\Phi_u$ be a norm-continuous family of finite interactions on $\mathbb Z^d$, indexed by $u\in[0,T]$, with $M_G:=\sup_{u\in[0,T]}\|\Phi_u\|_G<\infty$. For finite $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$, define $H_\Lambda(u)=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi_u(Z)$ and let $U_\Lambda(0)=I$ solve

$$\frac{d}{du}U_\Lambda(u)=-iH_\Lambda(u)U_\Lambda(u)/\hbar.$$

Set $\alpha_u^\Lambda(A)=U_\Lambda(u)^* A U_\Lambda(u)$, extended by the identity outside $\Lambda$. If $A\in\mathcal A_X$, $B\in\mathcal A_Y$ for disjoint finite nonempty $X,Y\subset\Lambda$, then

$$\|[\alpha_u^\Lambda(A),B]\|\le \frac{2\|A\|\|B\|}{C_G} \left(e^{2C_GM_Gu/\hbar}-1\right) \sum_{x\in X,\,y\in Y}G(d_\infty(x,y)).$$

The same estimate holds for the inverse path. In particular, for a constant interaction $\Phi$ evolved in physical time $t$ by $\tau_t^{\Lambda,\Phi}$, take $u=|t|$ and the constant path $\Phi_u=\Phi$ to obtain

$$\|[\tau_t^{\Lambda,\Phi}(A),B]\|\le \frac{2\|A\|\|B\|}{C_G} \left(e^{2C_G\|\Phi\|_G|t|/\hbar}-1\right) \sum_{x\in X,\,y\in Y}G(d_\infty(x,y)).$$

In physical units, $u,T,t$ are times, $M_G$ and $\|\Phi\|_G$ have energy units, and $\hbar$ has energy-times-time units; the weights and convolution constants are dimensionless, so the exponential arguments are dimensionless.

Let $X,Y\subset\mathbb Z^d$ be finite regions and $A\in\mathcal A_Y$. Embed $A$ in $\mathcal A_{X\cup Y}$, use the canonical site-order permutation to group factors in $X\cap Y$ and $Y\setminus X$, and apply the normalized trace on the omitted factors:

$$E_X(A):=\bigl(\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal A_{X\cap Y}}\otimes \tau_{Y\setminus X}\bigr)(A)\otimes I_{X\setminus Y}\in\mathcal A_X,\qquad \tau_D:=q^{-|D|}\operatorname{Tr}_D.$$

The empty tensor factor has normalized trace $1$. Since $\tau_D(I_D)=1$, adding an identity factor does not change the result, so this formula consistently defines $E_X$ on the directed union $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$. This definition alone asserts no norm extension to its completion.

For every finite $X\subset\mathbb Z^d$, the map $E_X$ of the normalized-trace-expectation definition is a unital positive contraction on $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and has a unique contractive extension $E_X:\mathcal A\to\mathcal A_X$. For $B\in\mathcal A_Y$, $Y$ finite,

$$\|B-E_X(B)\|\le \sum_{z\in Y\setminus X}\ \sup_{\substack{V\in\mathcal A_{\{z\}}\\V^*V=VV^*=I}} \|[B,V]\|.$$

Use the finite local matrix algebras and isometric factor inclusions of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]] and [[lem-qsm-local-spin-inclusions-isometric]]. Identify $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ with its image in every larger finite-region algebra. The directed union

$$\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}:=\bigcup_{\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma,\ |\Lambda|<\infty}\mathcal A_\Lambda$$

is the algebra of **strictly local observables**. Its norm is $\|A\|=\|A\|_{\mathcal A_\Lambda}$ for any finite localization region $\Lambda$ of $A$; isometric inclusions make this independent of the chosen region. The **quasi-local spin algebra** is the norm completion

$$\mathcal A:=\overline{\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}}^{\,\|\cdot\|}.$$

The C*-algebra structure on this completion has product and adjoint extended continuously from the finite local matrix algebras. Countable Choice is assumed for the published existence theorem for metric completions; [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]] supplies the full extension argument using the finite C*-identity of [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]].

**No global Hilbert tensor product is selected.** “Quasi-local” means norm completion of the directed algebra of finite-region observables; it does not mean a chosen representation as operators on an infinite tensor-product Hilbert space. A local operator $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ may have more than one localization region. Disjoint finite local factors commute in their common finite tensor algebra.

Fix $d\ge1$, $q\ge1$, and finite regions $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ as in [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]]. Then the factor inclusion $\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}(T)=T\otimes I$ is an isometric unital $*$-homomorphism:

$$\|\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}(T)\|=\|T\|\qquad(T\in\mathcal A_\Lambda).$$

For nested finite regions $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'\subseteq\Lambda''$, the inclusions compose: $\iota_{\Lambda',\Lambda''}\circ\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}=\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda''}$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Cauchy-sequence completion. For the local spin system of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]], the normed $*$-algebra $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and its completion $\mathcal A$ of [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]] are well defined; $\mathcal A$ is a unital complex C*-algebra and $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is norm dense in it. If $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and $B\in\mathcal A_\Delta$ for disjoint finite regions $\Lambda,\Delta$, then $AB=BA$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, $D=\dim H\ge1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. With composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity and the induced operator norm, $\mathcal B(H)$ is a nonzero unital complex C*-algebra in the sense of [[def-c-star-algebra]]. In particular it is complete, $\|AB\|\le\|A\|\|B\|$, $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$, $\|A^*\|=\|A\|$ and $\|I\|=1$. The matrix $\|A\|^2I-A^*A$ is positive semidefinite and has a positive square root in $\mathcal B(H)$.

Every complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal B(H)\to\mathbb C$ that is positive, meaning $\omega(B^*B)\ge0$ for all $B$, has a unique positive semidefinite matrix $\rho$ such that $\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)$ for all $A$. It is bounded and satisfies

$$|\omega(A)|\le\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)\|A\|\quad(A\in\mathcal B(H)),\qquad \|\omega\|=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)=\omega(I).$$

Consequently the canonical states of [[def-state-on-a-c-star-algebra]] are exactly the trace pairings of density operators of [[def-qc-density-operator]]; for a positive functional, normalization $\omega(I)=1$ is equivalent to norm one. The result includes zero positive functionals, nonfaithful densities and $D=1$; it makes no infinite-dimensional density representation assertion.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the countable union of finite regions and the finite-dimensional state/density interface explicitly stated in Facts [F3]. Let $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, $d\ge1$, and $q\ge1$ be as in [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]]. For every sequence of algebraic states $\omega_n$ on the quasi-local spin algebra $\mathcal A$, there is a subsequence $\omega_{n_k}$ and an algebraic state $\omega$ such that $\omega_{n_k}(A)\to\omega(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$. Thus the state space is sequentially compact in the pointwise topology, meaning convergence on every fixed observable. The conclusion concerns functional values; it does not assert convergence of global density matrices or a global trace-class representation.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $\mathcal A$ be the unital quasi-local spin C*-algebra of [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]], whose C*-structure uses Countable Choice as in [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]]. An **infinite algebraic state** is a bounded complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal A\to\mathbb C$ satisfying $\omega(I)=1$ and $\omega(A^*A)\ge0$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$.

For each finite region $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$, the restriction $\omega|_{\mathcal A_\Lambda}$ is a finite-matrix state. By [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]], every positive normalized functional on a finite matrix algebra is represented by a unique density matrix. Define its **local density matrix** $\rho_\Lambda$ by

$$\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda}(\rho_\Lambda A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda),$$

where $\rho_\Lambda=\rho_\Lambda^*\ge0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda}\rho_\Lambda=1$. For $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, put $\Delta=\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda$ and use the configuration-basis factorization $\mathcal H_{\Lambda'}\cong\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes\mathcal H_\Delta$ of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]]. If $T\in\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}$, define its **partial trace over $\Delta$**, $\operatorname{Tr}_\Delta(T)\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$, by its matrix coefficients

$$\langle \operatorname{Tr}_\Delta(T)e_s,e_{s'}\rangle:=\sum_{t\in S_\Delta}\langle T(e_s\otimes e_t),e_{s'}\otimes e_t\rangle\qquad(s,s'\in S_\Lambda),$$

where $e_s$ and $e_t$ are the configuration basis vectors of $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ and $\mathcal H_\Delta$. The finite sums depend linearly on $T$, so they define a linear map $\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}\to\mathcal A_\Lambda$ with a unique output matrix for each $T$. Expanding both configuration-basis traces gives its pairing identity

$$\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda\!\left(A\operatorname{Tr}_\Delta(T)\right)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'}\!\left((A\otimes I_\Delta)T\right)\qquad(A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda),$$

with the common value given by

$$\sum_{s,s'\in S_\Lambda}\sum_{t\in S_\Delta}\langle A e_{s'},e_s\rangle\langle T(e_s\otimes e_t),e_{s'}\otimes e_t\rangle.$$

The pairing identity determines this matrix uniquely: if $D\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ pairs to zero with every $A$, taking the configuration-basis matrix units $A=E_{ji}$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(E_{ji}D)=\langle D e_j,e_i\rangle=0$ for every $i,j$, so $D=0$. The local densities are **consistent** when $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}(\rho_{\Lambda'})=\rho_\Lambda$. No density operator on a globally chosen Hilbert space is part of this definition.

This agrees with the canonical state convention of [[def-state-on-a-c-star-algebra]]: the finite restrictions have norm one by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]], giving $|\omega(A)|\le\|A\|$ on the dense local algebra and hence on its completion; evaluation at the norm-one identity gives $\|\omega\|=1$. Conversely a canonical state has local restrictions with density matrices of trace one, since the finite norm formula and continuity on the dense local algebra imply $\|\omega\|=\omega(I)$. No global density representation is asserted.

derivations.claim: For each $n$, [F2] gives a norm-continuous self-adjoint $D_n(s)$. The finite-dimensional matrix ODE $U_n'=iD_nU_n$, $U_n(0)=I$, has a solution by its uniformly convergent Picard series; differentiating $U_n^*U_n$ gives $U_n^*U_n=I$. Differentiate $Q_n(s):=U_n(s)^*P_n(s)U_n(s)$. Since $U_n'=iD_nU_n$, $U_n^{*'}=-iU_n^*D_n$, and $P_n'=i[D_n,P_n]$, the three terms in $Q_n'$ cancel. Hence $Q_n(s)=P_n(0)$, or $P_n(s)=U_n(s)P_n(0)U_n(s)^*$. If $\rho_0$ is a finite-volume band density at $s=0$, then $U_n\rho_0U_n^*$ is a band density at $s$. The normalized-trace expectation satisfies $E_{\Lambda_n}(U_n^*AU_n)=U_n^*E_{\Lambda_n}(A)U_n$, first on finite tensor products and then by continuity. Cyclicity [F9] therefore gives $\omega^\Lambda_{\rho_0}\circ\alpha_{n,s}=\omega^\Lambda_{U_n\rho_0U_n^*}$. The density/state correspondence [F7, F10] makes both extensions states on $\mathcal A$. Reversing $U_n$ proves equality of the finite-volume state sets in both directions.

By [F3], the generator interactions $\Psi_{\Lambda_n}$ have a common $F_\rho$-norm bound $K_\rho$ for every $\rho>d$. The path $U_n'=iD_nU_n$ is the Heisenberg flow of the interaction $-\Psi_{\Lambda_n}$ with $\hbar=1$; its inverse is the reversed path with the same norm bound.

For two finite-volume propagators $U_J,U_K$, set $F(u)=\alpha^J_{u,0}(\alpha^K_{s,u}(A))$. The composition rule gives $F(0)=\alpha^K_{s,0}(A)$ and $F(s)=\alpha^J_{s,0}(A)$. In the Duhamel integrand, the removed terms are exactly those $\Psi_{\Lambda_n}(Z,u)$ with $Z

Fix $d\ge1$, the site set $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, its max-coordinate metric $d_\infty$, and the local spin algebras $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ of the uniformly finite-dimensional spin system. A finite interaction is a family $\Phi(Z)=\Phi(Z)^*\in\mathcal A_Z$ indexed by finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$. For a finite $\Lambda\subset\Gamma$, define

$$H_\Lambda^\Phi:=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi(Z),\qquad \tau_t^{\Lambda,\Phi}(A):=e^{itH_\Lambda^\Phi/\hbar}Ae^{-itH_\Lambda^\Phi/\hbar},$$

where $\hbar>0$, $A$ is embedded in a common finite local algebra, and the finite sum is a self-adjoint matrix. When a path $\Phi_s$, $s\in[0,1]$, is used, each $\Phi_s(Z)$ is $C^1$ in matrix norm and the derivative is taken term by term.

For $r\ge0$ put $F(r)=(1+r)^{-d-1}$. The admissible weights used here are

$$F_a(r):=e^{-ar}F(r)\quad(a>0),\qquad F_\rho(r):=(1+r)^{-\rho}\quad(\rho>d).$$

For an admissible weight $G$, define the weighted interaction norm

$$\|\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma}\frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{\substack{Z\subset\Gamma\ {\rm finite,\ nonempty}\\x,y\in Z}}\|\Phi(Z)\|.$$

The derivative norm of a path is

$$\|\partial\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma} \frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{Z\ni x,y}|Z|\,\|\partial_s\Phi_s(Z)\|.$$

A finite-volume spectral band is a nonempty selected subset $\Sigma_\Lambda(s)\subseteq\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})$ together with the orthogonal projection onto the sum of its eigenspaces. It may be specified by an interval $I_\Lambda(s)$ with smoothly varying endpoints, in which case $\Sigma_\Lambda(s)=\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})\cap I_\Lambda(s)$. The band is uniformly isolated with gap $\gamma>0$ along a specified finite-volume exhaustion when

$$\operatorname{dist}\!\left(\Sigma_\Lambda(s),\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})\setminus\Sigma_\Lambda(s)\right)\ge\gamma$$

for every volume in that exhaustion and every $s\in[0,1]$. For spectral-flow arguments, the selected eigenvalues must also form a locally fixed spectral cluster: for each $s_0$, a contour in the resolvent set encloses exactly the selected eigenvalues for all $s$ in a neighborhood of $s_0$. In finite dimension this implies that its projection is $C^1$ when the Hamiltonian path is $C^1$. This cluster condition holds, for example, for the first $r_\Lambda$ eigenvalues counted with multiplicity when the integer $r_\Lambda$ is fixed along the path and the gap after them stays open. Uniform distance between the selected and unselected spectra alone does not prevent an interval from changing membership discontinuously. A ground band is such a band containing the lowest eigenvalue or a finite-volume cluster of lowest eigenvalues; no uniqueness is implicit.

For physical units, take interaction terms and Hamiltonians in joules, time in seconds, and $\hbar$ in joule-seconds. The path parameter $s$, lattice distance, and admissible weights are dimensionless; the interaction norm therefore has energy units and the derivative norm has energy units per dimensionless path parameter.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

and if $S\subseteq T$ and both are densely defined, then $T^*\subseteq S^*$.

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.
For $a\le b$, every continuous real function on $[a,b]$ is a uniform limit of polynomials.

nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the

4. the three integrals agree:

$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument. Let $K:D(K)\to\mathcal H$ be densely defined, self-adjoint and positive, meaning $\langle Kx,x\rangle\ge0$ for $x\in D(K)$. Let $(U_t)_{t\in\mathbb R}$ be a strongly continuous unitary group with generator $iK$: its strong derivative at zero exists exactly on $D(K)$ and equals $iKx$. The spectrum $\sigma(K)$ is the complement of the set of $z$ for which $K-z:D(K)\to\mathcal H$ has a bounded everywhere-defined inverse.

For every $x,y\in\mathcal H$ there is a finite complex Borel measure $\mu_{x,y}$ on $[0,\infty)$ such that

$$\langle U_t x,y\rangle=\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{itE}\,d\mu_{x,y}(E),\qquad |\mu_{x,y}|([0,\infty))\le\|x\|\,\|y\|.$$

The measures are sesquilinear in $(x,y)$, $\mu_x:=\mu_{x,x}$ is positive with total mass $\|x\|^2$, and every $\mu_{x,y}$ is carried by $\sigma(K)$. If $P_0$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\ker K$, then

$$\mu_{x,y}(\{0\})=\langle P_0x,y\rangle.$$

In particular, if $\sigma(K)\subseteq\{0\}\cup[g,\infty)$ with $g>0$, the measures $\mu_{(I-P_0)x,(I-P_0)y}$ are carried by $[g,\infty)$. Spectral measures and a projection-valued spectral resolution are not assumptions of this statement.

For $t>0$ and $\widehat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e(-x\xi)\,dx$,
$$\widehat{e^{-\pi t x^2}}(\xi)=t^{-1/2}e^{-\pi\xi^2/t}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable

$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. $$|\omega(A)|\le\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)\|A\|\quad(A\in\mathcal B(H)),\qquad \|\omega\|=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)=\omega(I).$$

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

Each $\alpha_t$ is a bijective complex-linear unital $*$-homomorphism (a $*$-automorphism), with inverse $\alpha_{-t}$. Strong continuity means $t\mapsto\alpha_t(A)$ is norm-continuous for every fixed $A\in\mathcal A$. This result does not assert that an infinite-volume Hamiltonian is an element of $\mathcal A$ or a bounded operator on a preselected infinite tensor-product Hilbert space.

Fix $d\ge1$, the site set $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, its max-coordinate metric $d_\infty$, and the local spin algebras $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ of the uniformly finite-dimensional spin system. A finite interaction is a family $\Phi(Z)=\Phi(Z)^*\in\mathcal A_Z$ indexed by finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$. For a finite $\Lambda\subset\Gamma$, define

$$H_\Lambda^\Phi:=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi(Z),\qquad \tau_t^{\Lambda,\Phi}(A):=e^{itH_\Lambda^\Phi/\hbar}Ae^{-itH_\Lambda^\Phi/\hbar},$$

where $\hbar>0$, $A$ is embedded in a common finite local algebra, and the finite sum is a self-adjoint matrix. When a path $\Phi_s$, $s\in[0,1]$, is used, each $\Phi_s(Z)$ is $C^1$ in matrix norm and the derivative is taken term by term.

For $r\ge0$ put $F(r)=(1+r)^{-d-1}$. The admissible weights used here are

$$F_a(r):=e^{-ar}F(r)\quad(a>0),\qquad F_\rho(r):=(1+r)^{-\rho}\quad(\rho>d).$$

For an admissible weight $G$, define the weighted interaction norm

$$\|\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma}\frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{\substack{Z\subset\Gamma\ {\rm finite,\ nonempty}\\x,y\in Z}}\|\Phi(Z)\|.$$

The derivative norm of a path is

$$\|\partial\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma} \frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{Z\ni x,y}|Z|\,\|\partial_s\Phi_s(Z)\|.$$

A finite-volume spectral band is a nonempty selected subset $\Sigma_\Lambda(s)\subseteq\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})$ together with the orthogonal projection onto the sum of its eigenspaces. It may be specified by an interval $I_\Lambda(s)$ with smoothly varying endpoints, in which case $\Sigma_\Lambda(s)=\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})\cap I_\Lambda(s)$. The band is uniformly isolated with gap $\gamma>0$ along a specified finite-volume exhaustion when

$$\operatorname{dist}\!\left(\Sigma_\Lambda(s),\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})\setminus\Sigma_\Lambda(s)\right)\ge\gamma$$

for every volume in that exhaustion and every $s\in[0,1]$. For spectral-flow arguments, the selected eigenvalues must also form a locally fixed spectral cluster: for each $s_0$, a contour in the resolvent set encloses exactly the selected eigenvalues for all $s$ in a neighborhood of $s_0$. In finite dimension this implies that its projection is $C^1$ when the Hamiltonian path is $C^1$. This cluster condition holds, for example, for the first $r_\Lambda$ eigenvalues counted with multiplicity when the integer $r_\Lambda$ is fixed along the path and the gap after them stays open. Uniform distance between the selected and unselected spectra alone does not prevent an interval from changing membership discontinuously. A ground band is such a band containing the lowest eigenvalue or a finite-volume cluster of lowest eigenvalues; no uniqueness is implicit.

For physical units, take interaction terms and Hamiltonians in joules, time in seconds, and $\hbar$ in joule-seconds. The path parameter $s$, lattice distance, and admissible weights are dimensionless; the interaction norm therefore has energy units and the derivative norm has energy units per dimensionless path parameter.

Let $d\ge1$, $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, and $d_\infty$ be the max-coordinate metric. For $F(r)=(1+r)^{-d-1}$, $F_a(r)=e^{-ar}F(r)$ with $a>0$, and $F_\rho(r)=(1+r)^{-\rho}$ with $\rho>d$, each weight $G\in\{F_a,F_\rho\}$ is summable on $\Gamma$. Its convolution constant

$$C_G:=\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma} \frac{\sum_{z\in\Gamma}G(d_\infty(x,z))G(d_\infty(z,y))} {G(d_\infty(x,y))}$$

is finite and positive. In particular, for all $x,y\in\Gamma$,

$$\sum_{z\in\Gamma}G(d_\infty(x,z))G(d_\infty(z,y)) \le C_G\,G(d_\infty(x,y)).$$

The constant $C_{F_a}$ may be taken to be the convolution constant $C_F$ of $F$, independently of $a$.

Let $G$ be either $F_a$, $a>0$, or $F_\rho$, $\rho>d$, as in the weighted-interaction definition. Let $\Phi_u$ be a norm-continuous family of finite interactions on $\mathbb Z^d$, indexed by $u\in[0,T]$, with $M_G:=\sup_{u\in[0,T]}\|\Phi_u\|_G<\infty$. For finite $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$, define $H_\Lambda(u)=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi_u(Z)$ and let $U_\Lambda(0)=I$ solve

$$\frac{d}{du}U_\Lambda(u)=-iH_\Lambda(u)U_\Lambda(u)/\hbar.$$

Set $\alpha_u^\Lambda(A)=U_\Lambda(u)^* A U_\Lambda(u)$, extended by the identity outside $\Lambda$. If $A\in\mathcal A_X$, $B\in\mathcal A_Y$ for disjoint finite nonempty $X,Y\subset\Lambda$, then

$$\|[\alpha_u^\Lambda(A),B]\|\le \frac{2\|A\|\|B\|}{C_G} \left(e^{2C_GM_Gu/\hbar}-1\right) \sum_{x\in X,\,y\in Y}G(d_\infty(x,y)).$$

The same estimate holds for the inverse path. In particular, for a constant interaction $\Phi$ evolved in physical time $t$ by $\tau_t^{\Lambda,\Phi}$, take $u=|t|$ and the constant path $\Phi_u=\Phi$ to obtain

$$\|[\tau_t^{\Lambda,\Phi}(A),B]\|\le \frac{2\|A\|\|B\|}{C_G} \left(e^{2C_G\|\Phi\|_G|t|/\hbar}-1\right) \sum_{x\in X,\,y\in Y}G(d_\infty(x,y)).$$

In physical units, $u,T,t$ are times, $M_G$ and $\|\Phi\|_G$ have energy units, and $\hbar$ has energy-times-time units; the weights and convolution constants are dimensionless, so the exponential arguments are dimensionless.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), the C*-algebra completion interface of [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]], and the finite-matrix positive square-root interface of [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]]. Let $\{\rho_\Lambda\}$ be a consistent family of finite local density matrices as in [[lem-qsm-consistent-local-states]], and let $\omega$ be its extended algebraic state on the unital quasi-local algebra $\mathcal A$. Then there are a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H_\omega$, a unital $*$-representation $\pi_\omega:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\omega)$, and a unit vector $\Omega_\omega$ cyclic for $\pi_\omega$ such that

$$\omega(A)=\langle \pi_\omega(A)\Omega_\omega,\Omega_\omega\rangle\qquad(A\in\mathcal A),$$

using the linear-first inner-product convention. Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\omega)$ is the space of bounded linear operators with its operator norm, a $*$-representation is a complex-linear map preserving products, adjoints and the identity, and cyclic means that $\{\pi_\omega(A)\Omega_\omega:A\in\mathcal A\}$ is norm dense in $\mathcal H_\omega$. The theorem asserts existence of a cyclic representation, not uniqueness up to unitary equivalence.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument. Let $K:D(K)\to\mathcal H$ be densely defined, self-adjoint and positive, meaning $\langle Kx,x\rangle\ge0$ for $x\in D(K)$. Let $(U_t)_{t\in\mathbb R}$ be a strongly continuous unitary group with generator $iK$: its strong derivative at zero exists exactly on $D(K)$ and equals $iKx$. The spectrum $\sigma(K)$ is the complement of the set of $z$ for which $K-z:D(K)\to\mathcal H$ has a bounded everywhere-defined inverse.

For every $x,y\in\mathcal H$ there is a finite complex Borel measure $\mu_{x,y}$ on $[0,\infty)$ such that

$$\langle U_t x,y\rangle=\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{itE}\,d\mu_{x,y}(E),\qquad |\mu_{x,y}|([0,\infty))\le\|x\|\,\|y\|.$$

The measures are sesquilinear in $(x,y)$, $\mu_x:=\mu_{x,x}$ is positive with total mass $\|x\|^2$, and every $\mu_{x,y}$ is carried by $\sigma(K)$. If $P_0$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\ker K$, then

$$\mu_{x,y}(\{0\})=\langle P_0x,y\rangle.$$

In particular, if $\sigma(K)\subseteq\{0\}\cup[g,\infty)$ with $g>0$, the measures $\mu_{(I-P_0)x,(I-P_0)y}$ are carried by $[g,\infty)$. Spectral measures and a projection-valued spectral resolution are not assumptions of this statement.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal A$ be a unital complex $C^*$-algebra with a strongly continuous automorphism group $\alpha_t$. Let $\pi:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ be a contractive unital $*$-representation on a separable Hilbert space, with linear-first inner product, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector. Suppose a strongly continuous unitary group $U_t$ implements $\pi(\alpha_t(A))=U_t\pi(A)U_t^*$, fixes $\Omega$, and has positive self-adjoint generator $iK$ satisfying

$$\ker K=\mathbb C\Omega,\qquad \sigma(K)\subseteq\{0\}\cup[g,\infty),\qquad g>0.$$

Write $\omega(A)=\langle\pi(A)\Omega,\Omega\rangle$. Let $A,B\in\mathcal A$ commute, put $f(t)=\omega([A,\alpha_t(B)])$, and suppose $|f(t)|\le L|t|$ for $|t|\le\eta$, for some finite $L$ and $\eta>0$. For every $q>0$, the scalar integral

$$I_q(A,B):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{e^{-qt^2}}{2\pi it}\,f(t)\,dt$$

is absolutely convergent, with any value assigned to its integrand at $t=0$, and satisfies

$$\left|\omega(AB)-\omega(A)\omega(B)-I_q(A,B)\right|\le\|A\|\,\|B\|e^{-g^2/(4q)}.$$

The gap is that of this infinite- or finite-dimensional representation; no finite-volume approximating gaps are assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Assume Countable Choice. For a densely defined linear operator $T$ on $H$ the
adjoint $T^*$ is well defined and linear with linear domain $D(T^*)$; $T^*$ is
closed; for every $z\in\mathbb C$
$$\operatorname{ran}(T-z)^\perp=\ker(T^*-\overline z),$$
and if $S\subseteq T$ and both are densely defined, then $T^*\subseteq S^*$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: A cyclic representation of the spin algebra is separable. Indeed, finite tuples of the countable lattice enumerate its finite subsets, and rational real/imaginary entries form a countable dense family in each finite local matrix algebra. Countable Choice permits their countable union. Density follows, for a $D\times D$ matrix, from $\|T\|\le D\max_{i,j}|T_{ij}|$, obtained by finite Cauchy–Schwarz. The resulting countable family is dense in the completion, and its vectors $\pi(A)\Omega$ are dense in the cyclic Hilbert space by contractivity. The cyclic representation supplied by [F3] has the same state pairings as any given cyclic representation: the map $[A]\mapsto\pi(A)\Omega$ preserves $\langle[A],[B]\rangle=\omega(B^*A)$ and extends by density to a unitary. Thus the chosen cyclic ground representation is a separable realization of the actual GNS state, with no extra representation hypothesis.

We verify the advertised finite-range instance of the commutator premise. If $\Phi$ has range $R$ and per-site norm bound $\kappa$, a pair separated by more than $R$ contributes no interaction term, while for a pair of distance at most $R$ the numerator of the weighted norm is at most $\kappa$. Hence $\|\Phi\|_{F_a}\le\kappa/F_a(R)<\infty$. The uniform finite-volume bound [F2] passes to the thermodynamic limit for each local $A,B$ and fixed $t$, by norm continuity of commutators. The group is isometric, so $\|[A,\alpha_t(B)]\|=\|[\alpha_{-t}(A),B]\|$, matching exactly the supplier's time/support convention. This establishes the stated constants without replacing a general infinite-volume gap by a finite-volume gap.

The cyclic restriction in the ground-state definition preserves positive energy. Let $\mathcal L=\overline{\pi(\mathcal A)\Omega}$ in a ground representation. Covariance and $U_t\Omega=\Omega$ imply that $U_t$ and $U_{-t}$ preserve $\mathcal L$; its orthogonal projection commutes with $U_t$. For $x\in D(K)$, difference quotients show that this projection preserves $D(K)$ and commutes with $K$. The generator domain inside $\mathcal L$ is dense: the vectors $h^{-1}\int_0^hU_tx\,dt$ lie in it and tend to $x$ for $x\in\mathcal L$, as their difference quotients give $iK$ equal to $(U_hx-x)/h$. The restriction is self-adjoint because $K\pm i$ are onto, their bounded inverses preserve $\mathcal L$ by the commuting projection, and the restricted symmetric operator has both ranges onto; directly, if $y$ is in its adjoint domain, solve $(K+i)x=(K_{\mathcal L}^*+i)y$ in $\mathcal L$, and the zero kernel of $K_{\mathcal L}^*+i$ forces $x=y$. It is positive by restriction. More generally, for every $z$ in the resolvent of $K$, commutation of the projection with $K$ on its domain implies commutation with $(K-z)^{-1}$: apply $(K-z)$ and its injectivity to the two candidate images. This inverse therefore restricts to the inverse on $\mathcal L$, so $\sigma(K_{\mathcal L})\subseteq\sigma(K)$ and the spectral gap is inherited, as is a simple ground kernel. The resolvent surjectivity follows from the self-adjoint closed-range estimate exactly as in the spectral-measure helper. Thus the definition using a possibly noncyclic representation agrees with its cyclic restriction, without a Stone or spectral-existence theorem.

Let $P_0$ be the ground-kernel projection in the separable representation. A unit vector $\psi\in\ker K$ satisfies $U_t\psi=\psi$, since its orbit derivative is $iU_tK\psi=0$. Its vector state $\eta_\psi(A)=\langle\pi(A)\psi,\psi\rangle$ is a positive-energy ground state using the same representation; step 1.3 also supplies its cyclic version if desired. Uniqueness gives $\eta_\psi=\omega$. Scaling and polarization inside $\ker K$ therefore yield $P_0\pi(A)P_0=\omega(A)P_0$ for every $A$. If $\psi\in\ker K$ is orthogonal to $\Omega$, this identity implies $\langle\pi(A)\Omega,\psi\rangle=0$ for every $A$. Cyclicity forces $\psi=0$. Since the fixed vector $\Omega$ has zero orbit derivative, $\Omega\in D(K)$ and $K\Omega=0$, so we have $\ker K=\mathbb C\Omega$. The alternative hypothesis stated in the theorem supplies this directly and needs no uniqueness argument.

Put $N=\|A\|\|B\|$ and $f(t)=\omega([A,\alpha_t(B)])$. The displayed Lieb–Robinson premise, $F_a(s)\le e^{-as}$ and $d_\infty(x,y)\ge r$ give $$|f(t)|\le\frac{2N}{C}|X||Y|e^{-ar}(e^{v|t|}-1),\qquad |f(t)|\le2N.$$ The first bound is $O(t)$ at zero, including $v=0$. The local observables commute by [F1], so all time-integral hypotheses in [F4] hold. The same estimates apply to the finite-range instance justified in step 1.2.

Apply [F4] using step 2.1. For any $q,\tau>0$, split its absolutely convergent integral at $|t|=\tau$. Step 2.2 gives the short-time bound $$\frac{2N|X||Y|}{\pi C}e^{-ar}\int_0^\tau\frac{e^{vt}-1}{t}dt\le\frac{2N|X||Y|}{\pi C}e^{-ar+v\tau},$$ by [F6], because $(e^{vt}-1)/t\le ve^{vt}$ and $e^{v\tau}-1\le e^{v\tau}$, with zero left side when $v=0$. On the long-time part the trivial bound gives $$\frac{2N}{\pi}\int_\tau^\infty\frac{e^{-qt^2}}t dt=\frac N\pi\int_{q\tau^2}^\infty\frac{e^{-u}}u du\le\frac{N}{\pi q\tau^2}e^{-q\tau^2}.$$ Adding the filter error $Ne^{-g^2/(4q)}$ bounds the connected correlation. These estimates use only the supplied dynamics and its infinite-volume ground representation.

Choose $\tau=ar/(v+g/2)$ and $q=g/(2\tau)$. They are positive for $r\ge1$ and $g,a>0$, even when $v=0$. Then $$ar-v\tau=q\tau^2=\frac{g^2}{4q}=\frac{ag}{2v+g}r=\mu r,\qquad \frac1{q\tau^2}=\frac{2v+g}{agr}.$$ Substitution into step 3.1 proves the displayed bound. Zero observables give $N=0$ and require no division by $N$. The independent finite-volume band multiplicity and transport statements on this page are unchanged; this proof adds no claim that a degenerate gapped state has ordinary connected clustering. The clock conversion $g=\gamma/\hbar$ gives exactly the units in the Statement.
